newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Pakistan football makers made to mend ways.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pakistan football makers made to mend ways.

text.p: Muhammad Javed takes three hours, a few needle pricks and 24 rupees ($0.60) to stitch a world-class soccer ball. It will sell in Europe for $50.
At 17, Javed is a master craftsman with years of experience. He was nine years old when he made his first soccer ball, but his hard-earned skills did not come without pain.
"My uncle taught me how to pass the stitches. Every time I tried I would prick my fingers and cry with pain, but I did not give up," Javed said with pride.
He showed his two needle-scarred thumbs. "It still hurts when you prick your finger, but I am used to it now," he said.
Sitting awkwardly on a low stool, he deftly pierced a small hole in two pieces of leather held tightly in a wooden clamp balanced between his knees.
He threaded two needles through the hole from each side and tugged the waxed thread in opposite directions by jerking his arms apart.

Mechanically, he repeated the exercise, sewing steadily with an occasional intake of breath when he pricked his fingers. Most stitchers like Javed work eight to 10 hours a day, to earn a meagre 72 rupees ($1.79) a day, producing three or four balls that retail at $25 to $75 abroad, depending on quality.

The work goes on in thousands of village homes in and around the border city of Sialkot, sports goods capital of Pakistan, which exported more than 35 million soccer balls to European and American markets in 1995.
But the unregulated piecework system, with no checks on child labour, is under threat from international pressure that has prompted multinational sports goods firms to take action.
Last month Nike Inc of the United States and Pakistan's Saga Sports Ltd launched a soccer ball stitching plant that they said would help curb child labour in the sports goods industry.

"Nike will not tolerate the use of under-age labour in the production of its products and this stitching centre, and the others that follow, will ensure that," Nike vice-president Matthew Wolff said at the opening of the plant in Say Yoke village, 20 km (12 miles) west of Sialkot.
The factory, employing 500 stitchers, is the first of its kind in Pakistan. Nike will sell its produce around the world.
Saga president Khurshid Soofi said his company had taken the lead in improving working conditions for soccer ball-makers and in ensuring that child labour was not used.
He said there was a danger that world concern about child labour and other alleged abuses in Pakistani industry could lead to thousands of adult workers also losing their livelihoods.
He said Saga planned to set up five other stitching centres by September 1997 and 10 more by December 1998.

Martha Benson, director of communications Asia Pacific for Nike International Ltd, said Nike planned to buy two million soccer balls from Saga in fiscal 1997/98 (July-June), up from 40,000 in 1995/96.
Reebok International Ltd announced last month that it was setting up a similar soccer ball factory in Sialkot and would guarantee that its soccer balls were made without child labour.

"Reebok is taking this step in response to a specific child labour situation that exists in Pakistan where most of the world's quality balls are produced," Peter Moore, senior vice president of Reebok's global soccer and rugby division said.
He said that in the Sialkot region, soccer ball panels had historically been taken from factories to stitching centres where up to 20 percent of the stitchers were children.
"We are a company with zero tolerance for the current situation," he said in a statement received by Reuters.
Sialkot Chamber of Commerce and Industry says that only six percent of soccer ball stitchers are children and the rest are over 14, the legal age limit for factory workers in Pakistan.

No official figures exist, but a survey carried out by the Labour Ministry in collaboration with the International Labour Organisation, released in October, said 3.6 million children aged five to 14 were working full time in Pakistan.

Pakistan, faced with scathing international criticism and threats of trade sanctions, has taken steps to curb child labour, but officials say total elimination is impossible in a country where poverty and illiteracy are rife.
In 1990, Pakistan ratified the U.N. Convention on the Rights of the Child that prohibits child labour, but legal experts say more legislation needs to be enacted to implement it.
